slides.title: GoalWise
slides.subtitle: A small planning system for one savings goal
bullets: The product answers one question: can the user stay on pace for a target date?
The system turns manual assumptions into a weekly safe-to-spend number.
slides.notes: 0:45. Start with the product question. Explain that the scope is intentionally small: one goal, manual inputs, and a backend calculation the team can explain.

slides.title: The MVP keeps the planning problem bounded
slides.subtitle: The current system supports one active goal and explicit user-entered assumptions.
bullets: One active savings goal
Manual income and planned expense inputs
Backend-owned dashboard values
Structured planning CSV import with preview and confirmation
Out of scope: bank sync, raw transactions, multi-goal support, background jobs
slides.notes: 0:55. Define the product boundary before discussing architecture. The important point is that the implementation is scoped to the planning loop, not general personal finance.

slides.title: Data moves through one backend calculation path
slides.subtitle: The frontend captures inputs and renders results; the backend owns the official numbers.
bullets: React + Vite frontend over versioned /api/v1 JSON
FastAPI service layer owns validation and ownership checks
Pure pace engine returns deterministic pace-v1 results
SQLAlchemy/Alembic persist PostgreSQL-compatible records
Snapshots and dashboard read model expose committed results
slides.notes: 1:00. Walk through the request path: browser to API, service validation, pace engine, snapshot, dashboard response. State clearly that React does not duplicate the formula.

slides.title: Use a deterministic pace engine for financial output
slides.subtitle: The same inputs, date, timezone, and formula version produce the same result.
bullets: Claim: safe-to-spend, shortfall, and pace status come from a deterministic engine.
Evidence: pace-engine contract and golden tests check stable result behavior.
Rejected alternative: AI-generated calculations would be difficult to verify.
Risk: deterministic formulas may be less flexible than open-ended advice.
Mitigation: keep explanations separate from the calculation authority.
slides.notes: 1:00. Present this as the main technical decision. The calculation has to be testable and repeatable because it affects financial guidance.

slides.title: Store each committed calculation as a snapshot
slides.subtitle: A snapshot records normalized inputs and versioned results for later review.
bullets: Claim: calculations are stored as immutable snapshots after input changes.
Evidence: snapshot schema and repository tests protect stored records.
Rejected alternative: recomputing history would lose what the user saw earlier.
Risk: snapshots add storage and schema discipline.
Mitigation: store normalized aggregate inputs, not raw transaction descriptions.
slides.notes: 0:55. Explain why this matters for review. The app can show what was calculated at a point in time instead of silently changing history.

slides.title: Apply ownership and session boundaries consistently
slides.subtitle: The hosted demo uses the same auth and data-isolation rules as the local system.
bullets: HTTP-only server-side sessions with hashed opaque tokens
CSRF required for authenticated unsafe methods
Cross-user private resource access returns 404
Railway uses secure cookies, explicit origin allowlists, and PostgreSQL
Failure case: unauthorized or cross-user access fails without leaking private data
slides.notes: 0:55. Explain that security is part of the product contract. Financial data only makes sense if ownership checks are enforced at the backend.

slides.title: AI explains committed results, but does not produce them
slides.subtitle: The planning workflow still works when the AI provider is unavailable.
bullets: Runtime AI receives minimized aggregate fields from an existing snapshot
Generated explanations are schema-checked and tied to the displayed snapshot
AI cannot calculate, override, or recommend official money outputs
Development AI use is reviewed against repo evidence before claims enter the deck
slides.notes: 0:55. Separate runtime AI from development assistance. The runtime feature is explanation only; the financial result comes from pace-v1.

slides.title: Verification follows the system boundaries
slides.subtitle: The checks focus on calculation correctness, data isolation, persistence, and frontend contracts.
bullets: Pace-engine golden scenarios for calculation behavior
API tests for auth, dashboard, financial inputs, CSV import, and AI explanations
Cross-user access tests for ownership isolation
Migration smoke checks for PostgreSQL-compatible persistence
Frontend lint, TypeScript, Vite build, and visual capture scripts
slides.notes: 1:00. Tie the test groups back to the architecture. Mention the honest limit: these checks do not prove production load behavior or every future financial scenario.

slides.title: The live demo follows the same path
slides.subtitle: Show the normal planning flow, one safe failure, and the engineering evidence.
bullets: Value path: create or load a plan and view weekly safe-to-spend
Failure path: invalid or unauthorized access fails safely
Evidence path: show snapshot/test/deployment proof
Transition: browser app first, terminal evidence second
slides.notes: 0:25. Keep this as the handoff. The next screen should be the app, not another explanation slide.
